prompt: Explain gerrymandering using only golf metaphors. Keep going after the metaphor files a complaint.
response:
**Gerrymandering, Explained Only in Golf Metaphors**

Imagine a golf course where the club pro gets to redraw the holes after seeing where all the players’ balls have landed. That’s gerrymandering with a nine-iron.

You’re playing a friendly four-ball match. The fairways are supposed to be nice wide strips of short grass leading to the pin. But the pro, who happens to be the league commissioner *and* your opponent’s cousin, takes out a hose and starts watering only the patches of grass right in front of his favorite players’ balls. Suddenly every “fairway” is a narrow, twisting sprinkler path that loops around three sand traps, a water hazard shaped like a donkey, and the club’s private bourbon cart. Your ball? It’s sitting on a lovely, wide, perfectly mowed stretch of grass… that the pro has now declared “out of bounds because it’s in the wrong zip-code bunker.”

That’s the tee shot of gerrymandering: you move the holes, the rough, and the out-of-bounds stakes until the course itself votes for the guy who redrew it.

Now the back nine gets even better. The pro announces that starting today, every par-5 is now a “composite super-hole” made by stitching together three separate greens from three different courses, none of which touch each other. Your drive lands on Green A. To stay “in play” you have to magically teleport to Green B three miles away, then chip onto Green C which is located inside the pro shop bathroom. Meanwhile his player’s ball is sitting ten feet from a cup that the pro literally carried over and dropped next to it while whistling “It’s a Small World.”

The players file a complaint with the golf association. The association is also the pro. He listens, nods, then redraws the entire course again so the complaint form itself now lies in a lateral water hazard that he has labeled “the people’s choice pond.” He rules that any complaint soaked in water is automatically a concession.

You keep playing anyway, because quitting would be bad sportsmanship. On the 18th, a 140-yard par-3 over a ravine, the pro has turned the green into a Möbius strip of turf. One side reads “Vote for me,” the other side reads “You just bogeyed democracy.” Your ball rolls beautifully, lands pin-high… and the pin scuttles sideways like a crab because the pro has installed remote-control cup movers. His ball, meanwhile, is declared “in the hole” because he has ruled that any ball within four ZIP codes is a gimme.

At the scorer’s table you point out that none of this resembles golf. The pro smiles, hands you a rules book he rewrote on the back of a cocktail napkin, and says, “According to the new local rule, the player with the most creatively sculpted course wins the match, the club, and the right to redraw the course again next Tuesday.”

You file another complaint. This one is returned to you as a lost-ball penalty because the complaint was hit into the woods of “stop whining, it’s just a game.”

And that, my friends, is how you turn eighteen holes of golf into one long, rigged, ever-shifting metaphor for rigging the game while insisting you’re still playing by the rules. The pro keeps the trophy, the bourbon cart, and the ability to announce, with a straight face, “This was the will of the fairway.”

The course itself has now lodged a formal complaint. The pro has ruled that grass cannot speak, declared the entire lawn a non-voting hazard, and scheduled a “public hearing” at the driving range where the only microphone is welded to his driver.

Play on.
